newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean police step up pressure on strike leaders. [CORRECTED 3:57 GMT]
newsitem.headline: S.Korean police step up pressure on strike leaders. [CORRECTED 3:57 GMT]

text.p: South Korean riot police saturated the area around Seoul's Myongdong Cathedral on Friday, checking cars heading towards the church where seven labour leaders are sheltering from arrest.

Riot officers armed with clubs and shields peered into passenger windows and opened car trunks at a time of conflicting signals over whether authorities would use force to flush out the seven shaven-headed unionists.
Overnight, the situation was calm after around 10,000 people converged on the turn-of-the-century church but were turned back by large numbers of riot police and clouds of tear gas.
Later, union organisations staged a street concert outside the church with rock bands and dancers.
Officials have repeatedly said police would not storm the cathedral without the permission of Roman Catholic leaders.

But they have also made clear the law will be upheld. Four union heads have already been seized and arrest warrants are in force for 16 others, including the seven leaders of the Korean Confederation of Trade Unions.

In what is widely viewed as an ominous warning of a crackdown, authorities have linked labour strife to North Korea and produced Communist propaganda from Pyongyang they say is circulating among strikers.
The two Koreas have been technically at war since their 1950-53 conflict ended in a truce.

More than three weeks of sporadic work stoppages were sparked by the passage of a new labour law that gives employers the right to lay off workers, replace strikers and extend work hours. It was rammed through the National Assembly on December 26 in a secret dawn session.

International labour organisations stepped up their pressure on South Korea to dump the law, which they maintain curbs worker rights to freedom of association by allowing the Federation of Korean Trade Unions to retain its monopoly on union representation until 2000.
Ten leaders of trade union organisations from around the world are to due to arrive next week to replace four others who left on Thursday.
South Korea's immigration chief said the 10 would be allowed in, but warned they would be deported if they took part in strike-related protests.
"Immigration officers will explain our laws to the new visitors on their arrival in view of the illegal activities by the four foreign union leaders," Yu Byong-rahng told Reuters.
"There will first be warnings if they violate laws and if they continue not to heed them, then they will be deported."

The Geneva-based International Federation of Commercial and Clerical Workers said the 10-member team would observe strikes. It would be headed by Bill Jordan of the International Confederation of Free Trade Unions.
The labour ministry said strikes were winding down.
"With workers returning to work places in smaller companies, the number of participants in strikes is reducing," said ministry official Lee Young-shik.
He said 57,320 workers at 48 companies were on strike on Friday.
"It looks as if the strikes are in a lull but it is too early to talk about a trend now," he said.
Meanwhile, a trade ministry official warned that strikes could push South Korea's January trade deficit to a monthly high if they continued.

The shortfall for January could hit $3.9 billion from an earlier forecast of $3.2 billion and $2.13 billion last January. The previous record shortfall was $3.28 billion in August 1996, the official said.
"Export losses from the strikes are currently at around $441 million, and we see that rising to $645 million by the end of the month," he added. (Corrects from billions to millions)
